title: Pull a reject bin from the middle of a gravity flow lane without letting the next bin run down
instruction: Put the red-tagged bin in the reject tote. Until it is in the tote, the next bin up the lane must not move more than 2 cm. At the end, the other three bins must be down against the front stop and each other, with nothing holding them.
context: Stockers and order fillers (O*NET 53-7065.00; about 2.8 million US jobs, BLS) pick from carton-flow racks and pull out stock put on quality hold, which can be any bin in a lane. A carton-flow lane has no motor: it is a bed of free-running wheels sloped down to a front stop, so gravity brings each bin forward when the one ahead is taken. When a bin is lifted out of the middle, the bins behind it start rolling at once; they can catch under the lifted bin or the hand and run into the bin ahead. A stocker holds the next bin with the other hand until the reject is out, then lets it roll down so the lane closes up. The instruction gives the limits, not this way of meeting them.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. The robot works the lane from its side, as a worker does a flow lane running along a kitting bench. Lane (fixed to the table): one gravity carton-flow lane with no motor, running along y at x 26 and sloping down 3 degrees toward -y (real carton flow falls 0.5 to 0.75 in. per foot, 2.4 to 3.6 degrees). Its bed is three rows of black plastic skate wheels, 2 cm across and every 4 cm, on steel tracks at x 22, 26 and 30; the wheel tops are 4 cm above the table at the stop and 7.0 cm at the loading end, 58 cm up the lane (y 23.9). Two steel guide rails, 0.7 cm thick and 2.5 cm above the wheels, are 12 cm apart inside (x 20 to 32). A yellow steel front stop, 1.2 cm thick and 4 cm tall, closes the low end, its face at y -34. The lane stands on two steel cross bars with legs, 3 cm from each end. Bins: four blue polypropylene small-parts shelf bins, 13.7 x 10.5 x 7.6 cm (the common 30210 size), 3 mm walls, each with its 4.5 cm tall hopper front facing down the lane and its long side along the lane. Each holds a plastic bag of 1/4-20 zinc hex bolts (6 x 10 x 2.5 cm); bin and bolts weigh 0.35 kg. They stand nose to tail, 1 mm apart, from the stop: slot 1 (the front bin, against the stop) has its middle at y -27.1, slot 2 at y -13.3, slot 3 at y 0.5 and slot 4 at y 14.3. The tagged bin, with a red tag 5 x 7.5 cm on its bolts and a red band on its hopper front, is in slot 2 or slot 3, drawn at random with equal odds each time the task loads; the other three carry white labels. The next bin up the lane is the one just behind the tagged bin (slot 3 or 4). Reject tote (fixed): red polypropylene, 18 x 26 x 10 cm outside, 4 mm walls, open top, on the table behind the lane's low end with its middle at x 42, y -25; its near wall is 0.3 cm behind the far guide rail.
scoring: What counts is how far the next bin up the lane moves from its start, in any direction, until the tagged bin is in the tote (middle inside the tote's walls, bottom below the rim); after that it is meant to roll down. The tagged bin is placed when it rests on the tote's floor (bottom within 1.5 cm of it, not on the rim), upright within 20 degrees (not propped on a wall), let go and still for 1 second. The lane is closed up when the other three bins sit flat on the wheels (within 10 degrees and 1 cm) in their order, the first within 1 cm of the stop and each of the others within 1 cm of the bin ahead (1 cm allows for the bins' molded draft), still and let go. Still means under 1 cm/s and 10 degrees/s. With the tagged bin placed: 1.0 if the next bin moved at most 2 cm and the lane is closed up for 1 second; 0.75 if it moved at most 2 cm but the lane is not closed up; 0.5 if it moved over 2 cm and at most 8 cm (it began to run and was caught); 0.25 if it moved over 8 cm (more than half of the 13.7 cm gap). Otherwise 0, including doing nothing. A lane bin (one of the three untagged bins) that falls (outside the lane, moving down faster than 0.5 m/s, not a set-down) makes the whole trial 0. A lane bin off the lane at the end (its middle outside the guide rails or past either end) or tipped past 30 degrees (gone over, not rocking) also scores 0; one stood back on the wheels counts again. Why 2 cm: a hand closing on a bin's wall moves it about 1 cm, while a bin that starts to run passes 2 cm in under half a second. Any way of staying within 2 cm counts, including a very quick one-hand lift; holding the next bin doesn't depend on speed. In a real trial, tape a paper scale marked every 1 cm on the near guide rail beside the next bin and film from a side camera at table height; read the next bin's movement from the paused video, the end gaps with a ruler, and the tagged bin's seat and tilt from a photo.
reset_notes: Stand the four bins back nose to tail against the stop with their bags of bolts, the tagged bin in slot 2 or 3 (toss a coin for each trial). Nothing is consumed. Before each trial, check that a bin set at the loading end rolls down to the stop on its own.
fidelity: Real size and mass. The skate wheels are drawn but not simulated: the bed is one flat surface with friction 0.03, below the 3-degree slope's 0.052, so a free bin runs down at about 0.22 m/s^2, as on free-running wheels. The bins are rigid with straight walls (real ones taper slightly), and each bag of bolts is a solid block fixed in its bin. The lane and tote are fixed.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (2,400 steps); demo: 1.0 (411 steps with the tag in slot 2, 409 in slot 3)
